summary:
Querétaro de Arteaga stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. A Human Rights Watch backgrounder dated 31 March 2025 records that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, and the organisation's state-by-state table lists Querétaro among the six states that have never legislated any such procedure. A trans visitor to Querétaro therefore has no local administrative route to align identity documents with lived identity: the papers carried on arrival are the only identification available, and they cannot be corrected there.

The documented consequence of that absence is mistreatment. Human Rights Watch's report of 6 March 2024, "I Just Want to Contribute to Society", co-authored with a local trans community organisation, finds that the absence of any gender-recognition procedure in Tabasco exposes trans people to police and institutional mistreatment, and names Tabasco the clearest case among the six states whose legislatures refuse any procedure. The same report found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

Querétaro has moved in the opposite direction on one specific measure. The reform to Querétaro's Penal Code prohibiting Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual y la Identidad de Género (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies, was published and is in force, as reported by Tribuna de Querétaro on 20 September 2023. It carries two to six years in prison, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, treating such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture.

Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal in Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. The gap between statute and practice is the recurring finding on protection more broadly. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against trans people nationally sets the background against which document mismatch matters. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City; the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap: Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide, taking its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished. Inter-American authorities have pressed the wider point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Tabasco serves as the comparison case for Querétaro's own gap, since both are among the six states legislatures that refuse any recognition procedure, and Human Rights Watch singles out Tabasco as the clearest instance of the resulting exposure. The Human Rights Watch report of 31 March 2025 also notes that implementation of recognition procedures differs sharply from one state to another even where procedures exist.
localsOnly:
Residents of Querétaro who are subjected to conversion practices have a published and enforceable Penal Code prohibition to rely on, with penalties of two to six years in prison, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service. The prohibition frames such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture.

Local anti-discrimination advocates treat the ban as a milestone, particularly measured against states where an equivalent ban remains unpublished, while stating that a first generation of LGBTIQ+ reforms is still pending in Querétaro. The spokesman for the Frente Queretano por el Derecho a la No Discriminación, Walter López, made that assessment in Tribuna de Querétaro on 20 September 2023. Residents seeking to correct name and gender markers on identity documents have no state-level administrative procedure to apply to, since Querétaro's legislature has never created one.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Querétaro courts have granted legal gender recognition case by case through constitutional or judicial routes, given the absence of any administrative procedure, is not resolved in the sources assembled here.

No information in the inventory documents whether the ECOSIG prohibition has been enforced in Querétaro since publication, whether complaints have been filed, or what outcomes followed; the penalty provisions are sourced, enforcement is not.

Whether hate-crime enhancement applies to offences against trans victims in Querétaro, and how prosecutors there treat document mismatch as an aggravating or mitigating factor, is not sourced.

The status and content of the further LGBTIQ+ legislative reforms that local advocates describe as pending in Querétaro are not specified in the inventory, and their progress after September 2023 is unresolved.

Human Rights Watch's March 2025 map counts Querétaro among states that have never legislated a recognition procedure; whether any draft bill was before the Querétaro Congress at that date is not stated.
